strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning four diverse datasets (indoor/outdoor, handheld/drone/robot) against 13 baselines including classical VIO, learning-based VO, visual Gaussian Splatting SLAM, and visual-inertial systems, providing a thorough and convincing comparison landscape.

Strong and consistent quantitative improvements in tracking accuracy (ATE RMSE) and rendering quality (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS) across nearly all tested sequences, with results reported both with and without final global BA/color refinement for fair 'online' comparison.

Well-designed robustness experiments (strided frame-dropping evaluation and a self-captured extreme-condition sequence) that directly and convincingly validate the paper's central claim that IMU fusion improves resilience to degraded visual conditions, which purely visual 3DGS baselines clearly fail under.

Systematic ablation studies isolating the contribution of IMU fusion, loop closure, keyframe initialization strategy, and the loop-closure Gaussian update, each showing meaningful degradation when removed.

Detailed engineering contributions (staged IMU initialization, time-varying bias modeling with temporal smoothness term, PGBA-based loop closure with efficient batched Gaussian pose/scale propagation) are clearly described with sufficient mathematical detail and implementation specifics (thresholds, hyperparameters) in the supplementary to aid reproducibility.
Extensive supplementary material with per-sequence breakdowns, runtime analysis, and dataset statistics enhances transparency and evidentiary support for the claims.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is primarily integrative rather than fundamental: the visual front-end is directly inherited from DROID-SLAM, the inertial residual formulation closely follows standard IMU-preintegration approaches (e.g., ORB-SLAM3/VI-DSO style), and the loop-closure PGBA is adapted from HI-SLAM2; the main contribution is the careful combination and staged optimization of these known components rather than a new algorithmic idea.

Despite being framed as a 'real-time' system, reported frame rates (4-16 FPS with mapping) are slower than the purely-visual HI-SLAM2 baseline, and the authors acknowledge the IMU code is not yet CUDA-optimized, undermining the real-time claim in its current form.

Comparison with the most directly relevant prior work (VINGS-Mono, a visual-inertial 3DGS SLAM system) is largely deferred to related-work discussion rather than included in the main experimental tables; MM3DGS-SLAM results are copied from its paper rather than reproduced under the same protocol, limiting the fairness/completeness of head-to-head comparison with the closest competitors.

The 'extreme conditions' robustness claim rests on a single self-captured sequence with pseudo ground truth from another SLAM system (FAST-LIVO2), which is a relatively weak and potentially circular form of validation given limited sample size.

No code release is confirmed at submission time (project page mentioned but link omitted), and given the system's complexity (multi-stage initialization, joint BA, PGBA, Gaussian update propagation), independent reproducibility without released code would be challenging.

Some robustness/ATE metrics under strided evaluation show known pitfalls (e.g., low ATE with very low recall for baselines), which the paper appropriately discusses, but this also highlights that ATE alone is an imperfect metric throughout the rest of the paper's main tables where only ATE is reported.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored gap: existing 3DGS SLAM systems are almost exclusively vision-only, and the paper provides one of the more complete attempts at tightly coupling IMU with dense visual correspondence-based tracking and Gaussian mapping.

Extensive experimental evaluation across four diverse datasets (EuRoC, RPNG AR Table, UTMM, FAST-LIVO2) spanning indoor/outdoor and handheld/drone/robot capture, with comparisons to 13 baselines covering classic VIO, learning-based VO, and 3DGS SLAM families.

Strong quantitative results in tracking accuracy (ATE RMSE) and rendering quality (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS), often ranking first or second, and the method is notably one of the few that avoids failure across all sequences in the harder datasets.

Thoughtful robustness experiments beyond standard benchmarks, including strided-frame evaluation to simulate frame drops/high-speed motion and a self-captured extreme-condition sequence, along with sensible use of Recall metrics to avoid the pitfalls of ATE on partially-tracked trajectories.

Reasonably thorough ablations isolating the contribution of IMU fusion, loop closure, keyframe initialization strategy, and the loop-closure Gaussian update, with clear degradation shown when each component is removed.

Good transparency in reporting: results both before/after final global BA and color refinement, detailed per-sequence tables in supplementary, and explicit disclosure of which baseline numbers are reproduced vs. copied from original papers.
weaknesses: Real-time claims in the abstract/title are not well supported by the reported runtime: the full system (tracking + mapping) runs at roughly 4-11 FPS on an RTX 5090, and the authors themselves note that IMU-related code is unoptimized NumPy rather than CUDA, undermining the practical real-time positioning central to the paper's framing.

The core technical contribution is largely an integration of existing components (DROID-SLAM visual frontend, standard IMU preintegration formulation following Forster et al./ORB-SLAM3-style residuals, and HI-SLAM2-inspired pose-graph BA for loop closure) rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic idea; the novelty is more architectural/systems-level than conceptual.

VINGS-Mono, described in related work as one of the closest prior VI-3DGS SLAM systems, is never benchmarked quantitatively in the experiments despite being a natural and important comparison point; its omission weakens the empirical case against the most relevant competing method.

Several baseline numbers (e.g., SVO, TartanVO, DSO, some VIO methods on EuRoC) are copied from other papers rather than reproduced under the authors' own evaluation protocol, which can introduce inconsistencies in evaluation setup (e.g., different hardware, trajectory alignment, or metric conventions) that are not fully controlled for.

The extreme-condition robustness claim rests on a single self-captured sequence with pseudo ground truth from another SLAM system (FAST-LIVO2), which is a weak statistical basis for a general robustness claim and also introduces potential circularity/bias since the pseudo-GT method itself has its own error characteristics.

Limited discussion of failure modes or limitations of the proposed fusion itself (e.g., behavior under large/rapidly varying IMU bias, degenerate motion, or IMU-dominant scenarios); the stated limitations section is brief and focused mainly on hardware/camera-setup constraints rather than algorithmic failure cases.

Comparison methodology partially favors the proposed method by evaluating online (pre-refinement) performance for Gaussian-splatting baselines while some classical VIO baselines may use different operating assumptions; although disclosed, this makes head-to-head comparisons less clean and could be seen as advantaging the proposed pipeline's staged design.
